```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(patchwork)
library(hexbin)
```

## Question 1
```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
summary(ny_noaa)
```
This data set has `r nrow(ny_noaa)` rows and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` columns. Key variables include, id, date, prcp, snow, snwd, tmax, and tmin. There are quite a lot of NA values, especially in the tmax and tmin variables. 

```{r}
# Data Cleaning and Converting Units
ny_noaa <- 
  ny_noaa |> 
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    year = year(date),
    month = month(date),
    day = day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10, 
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )
summary(ny_noaa)

# prcp: Precipitation (tenths of mm)
# snow: Snowfall (mm)
# temp: (tenths of degrees C)
```

```{r}
ny_noaa |> 
  count(snow, sort = T)
```
For snowfall, the most commonly observed value is 0, because it doesn't snow most days of the year. 

```{r}
ny_noaa |> 
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |>      # Jan or July only
  group_by(id, year, month) |>      # per each station and year
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = T), .groups = "drop") |>     # dropping NA to remove clutter
  drop_na(mean_tmax) |> 
  mutate(month = factor(month, levels = c(1, 7), labels = c("January", "July"))) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.1) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(x = "Year", 
       y = "Mean max temperature Celsius",
       title = "Average Max Temperature in January vs July, per station")+
  theme_classic()
```
From these plots, we can see that the average max temperature in January is much lower compared to July. In January, the range is from about 10°C to below -10°C. In July it is as hot as over 30°C to about 20°C, with an outlier of ~14°C.

```{r, fig.width = 14, fig.height = 8}
# tmax vs tmin
p1 <- ny_noaa |> 
  drop_na(tmax, tmin) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex() +
  labs(x = "tmin Celsius", 
       y = "tmax Celsius", 
       title = "Max Temp vs Min Temp") +
  theme_classic()

# snowfall 
p2 <- ny_noaa |> 
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |> 
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "year", 
       y = "snowfall (mm)", 
       title = "Snowfall Between 0 and 100 mm") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 3, hjust = 3))
  
p1 + p2
```
There is a a strong positive relationship between tmax and tmin. The cluster is dense in moderate temps of about 0 - 15 Celsius minimum, and 10 - 25 Celsius maximum.
For snowfall, the shape is similar across years, with most values being small values. A few years that stand out however, are 1997, 2003, 2005, 2006, and 2009. 



## Question 2
```{r}
nhanes_accel <- read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names()
nhanes_covar <- read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |> 
    janitor::clean_names()
```

```{r}
# cleaning 
nhanes_df <- 
  nhanes_covar |> 
  drop_na() |>                       # drop people wiht missing demographic data
  filter(age >= 21) |>               # adults 
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), 
                 labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    education = factor(education, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                       labels = c("Less than high school", 
                                  "High school equivalent", 
                                  "More than high school"))
  ) |> 
  inner_join(nhanes_accel, by = "seqn") 
```

# table of men and women by education
```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  count(education, sex) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n) |> 
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Education", "Male", "Female"))
```

# age distribution by sex and education 
```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Education", y = "Age ", fill = "Sex",
       title = "Age Distribution in years by Sex and Education")
```

# total activity by age
```{r}
nhanes_df <- 
  nhanes_df |> 
  mutate(total_activity = rowSums(across(starts_with("min"))))

nhanes_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = F) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Total daily activity", color = "Sex",
       title = "Total Activity by Age, by Sex and Education") 
```
In the More than high school group, women are more active than men at most ages, with the gap narrowing in later life.
Across all three education levels, total daily activity declines with age, especially around the age of 60. In the High School Equivalent group, women are generally more active than men as well. In the Less the High School group, the activity is led by women, with men being more active after the age of about 40. 

# 24 Hr plot
```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  pivot_longer(starts_with("min"), 
               names_to = "minute", 
               names_prefix = "min", 
               values_to = "mims") |> 
  mutate(hour = as.numeric(minute) / 60) |> 
  group_by(education, sex, hour) |> 
  summarize(mean_mims = mean(mims), .groups = "drop") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, 
             y = mean_mims, 
             color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  geom_smooth(se = F) +
  labs(x = "Hour of day", 
       y = "Average activity", 
       color = "Sex",
       title = "Daily Activity by Education and Sex") + 
  theme_classic()
```
In all three education groups, the mean activity througout the day is about the same. Activity is lowest around 4am and riced between 5 am and 9 am. In the High schol equivalent and more than high school groups, there is a bit of deviation from the mal and femlale groups, with females have higher mean activity. It is hard to tell is higher education is associated with more daytime actifiy level, but there does seem to be the most acitivty in the less than high school group. 

## Question 3

```{r}
jan_2020 = 
  read_csv("data/Jan2020Citi.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(year = "2020", month = "January")

july_2020 = 
  read_csv("data/July2020Citi.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(year = "2020", month = "July")

jan_2024 = 
  read_csv("data/Jan2024Citi.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(year = "2024", month = "January")

july_2024 = 
  read_csv("data/July2024Citi.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(year = "2024", month = "July")

citi_df = 
  bind_rows(jan_2020, july_2020, jan_2024, july_2024) |> 
  mutate(weekdays = factor(weekdays, levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", 
                                                "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")))
```
The combined dataset has `r nrow(citi_df)` rides and `r ncol(citi_df)` variables, 
from January and July of 2020 - 2024. The variables for each ride contain an ID, bike type, day of the week, duration in minutes, start/end station, rider type member/casual. For tidyness, I added a month and year variable. 

# rides by month year, ride type
```{r}
citi_df |> 
  count(year, 
        month, 
        member_casual) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = member_casual, values_from = n) |> 
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("year", " month", "casual", "member"))
```

# top 5 start stations , July 2024
```{r}
citi_df |> 
  filter(year == "2024", month == "July") |> 
  count(start_station_name, sort = T) |> 
  head(5) |> 
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("start station", "Num Rides"))
```

# plot, median duration 
```{r}
citi_df |> 
  group_by(year, 
           month, 
           weekdays) |> 
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration), .groups = "drop") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, color = year)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(group = year)) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(x = "Day of week", y = "Median ride in minutes", color = "Year",
       title = "Median Ride Duration by Day, Month, and Year") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))
```
Ride durations are much longer in July than in January, with with the weekends have a longer ride than during the weekday. In July 2020, there was a dip on Friday, from what we can see. These things can be due to temperature and work schedules. Overall, 2020 ride durations are longer than 2024. 

# 2024 ride durations
```{r}
citi_df |> 
  filter(year == "2024") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = month, 
             y = duration, 
             fill = member_casual)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(. ~ rideable_type) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "month", y = "minutes", fill = "Rider type",
       title = "2024 ride durations by month, rider type, bike type")
```
I used the log scale for this plot for better readability. Casual riders take longer rides than members across every combinition of month and bike type. July rides are longer than January across both groups. Classic bikes have longer rides than electric bikes, especially in casual riders.
